source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving
finding: Warmth ratings (self-rated closeness to solution) were taken every 15 s. They rose gradually before correct answers on multistep and algebra problems, but changed little before correct answers on classic insight problems. The authors proposed using this suddenness to define insight.
numbers: Exp 1: 26 paid volunteers, 19 usable; 10 problems (5 multistep, 5 insight); 3 cm visual analogue scale, up to 40 ratings per problem. Gamma (insight vs noninsight incrementality): .26 angular warmth, t(18)=2.02; .23 differential warmth, t(18)=1.63, one-tailed.
quote: insight problems in Experiment 1 showed a more sudden achievement of solution than did those of the noninsight problems
limits: Small N; one-tailed test on the differential measure; problem type was fixed by prior labels, not measured per solver; only subjects with a correct answer and enough ratings counted.
agent_relevance: Founding evidence that a gradual feel of nearing the goal is a feature of some problems only. A monitor based on felt closeness cannot assume gradual growth.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving
finding: Exp 2 repeated the warmth contrast with algebra problems against insight problems, 15 s rating interval, 17 rating slots, set order counterbalanced. Algebra showed a gradual rise in warmth in the last minute; insight showed little rise.
numbers: 39 subjects with usable warmth data. Gamma for insight vs algebra: .35 angular, t(37)=3.10; .32 differential, t(37)=2.56. Figure 1 histograms at 60, 45, 30, 15 s before solution; a rating of 7 (of 7) was always given at solution.
limits: Usable data needed at least one insight and one algebra problem solved with 3 or more warmth ratings; many subjects dropped (the later literature counts 39 of 73 usable).
agent_relevance: Replicates Exp 1 with a cleaner contrast. The effect is moderate (gamma about .3), so warmth is a noisy signal.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving
finding: Feeling-of-knowing (predicting in advance which problems one will solve) worked for algebra but not for insight problems. Normative difficulty beat the solvers' own predictions.
numbers: Gamma of rank order vs solving: algebra G=.40 (t(46)=4.6, above 0), insight G=.08 (t(46)=.8, not above 0); difference F(1,46)=6.46. Normative difficulty predicted individuals' success: r=.77 insight, .60 algebra.
limits: Same-sample difficulty ranking gave each subject a 2.1% self-contribution to the norm.
agent_relevance: Self-prediction of success is poor on hard novel problems; use base rates by problem class from data rather than the model's own feeling. Supports code-set triggers over self-reports.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving
finding: The same paper describes the earlier Metcalfe (1986b) study: with warmth rated every 10 s on a 10-point scale, 78% of correct insight problems and anagrams rose by no more than 1 point over the whole interval. Wrong answers showed a more incremental rise.
numbers: 78% of correctly solved problems and anagrams (Metcalfe 1986b, as described here) had warmth rise of 1 point or less on a 10-point scale; incorrect solutions showed incremental patterns.
quote: On those problems for which the wrong answer was given, however, the warmth protocols showed a more incremental pattern.
limits: Second-hand description; the 1986b paper itself was not opened. The authors say the incremental pattern may reflect a decision strategy, not the solving process.
agent_relevance: Rising warmth can mark a wrong answer. High felt closeness is not a safe reason to stop; keep an external check.

source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving
finding: Theory behind the prediction: Simon, Newell and Shaw (1979) said people search in a directed way by comparing the current state with the goal. A move that makes the state more like the goal (warmer) is kept. This is means-end difference reduction. If it guides solving, warmth should climb steadily.
numbers: Predicts steadily rising warmth for problems modeled by search programs (Logic Theorist, Karat 1982). Observed for multistep and algebra problems in Exp 1 and 2.
limits: Authors admit their criterion for calling a problem 'insight' was not well defined; they dropped problems their subjects had rated 'grind-out'.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal root of progress monitoring: distance-to-goal comparison. This is the quantity a code rule can compute where a distance exists.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
finding: Non-replication of the warmth difference with 32 magic-trick videos. Warmth did not differ between trials solved with and without an Aha experience.
numbers: N=51 students (8 dropped for reporting no Aha), 971 trials kept. Differential warmth: insight M=2.92 (n=50) vs noninsight M=0.30 (n=162), t(210)=0.79, p=.429, d=.12. Angular warmth: .41 vs -.004, t(49.36)=1.12, p=.266, d=.22.
quote: these findings contrast with the earlier findings of Metcalfe and Wiebe
limits: About 70% of trials had too few (3 to 4) ratings and were dropped; 15 s videos; max 5 warmth ratings; participants were not required to be fully confident; insight was self-labeled by subject, not by problem type.
agent_relevance: Warmth suddenness is not a robust marker across paradigms. Do not build a trigger on a single sudden or gradual signature.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
finding: Insight-labelled solutions were more accurate and more confident than noninsight ones. Confidence tracked accuracy within both types.
numbers: Accuracy 0.57 vs 0.37, t(506.9)=5.78, d=.51. Confidence 78.32 vs 68.95, t(606.8)=6.17, d=.50. Solution time 38.23 vs 40.56 s, p=.089. 29% of trials were insight.
limits: Aha was self-reported after the solution; magic tricks may not generalise to classic insight problems.
agent_relevance: Felt certainty after a sudden solution is somewhat valid for humans; it cannot be assumed for a model.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
finding: Metacognitive discrimination (Az, how well confidence separates correct from incorrect) was near chance for insight solutions and above chance for noninsight solutions.
numbers: Az (33 participants): insight 0.56 vs noninsight 0.63, t(32)=1.06, p=.297. Insight Az vs chance: t(33)=1.51, p=.142. Noninsight Az 0.64, t(41)=5.43, p<.001.
limits: Difference between types was not significant; only the vs-chance contrast differs. Small subgroup.
agent_relevance: Confidence after sudden insight-like solutions barely separates right from wrong. Another reason to check outputs in code, not trust felt certainty.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
finding: The authors read Metcalfe (1986) as showing that high confidence just before an answer on insight problems predicted an error (people talk themselves into a wrong answer), and offer satisficing as the reason for incremental warmth when answers are wrong.
numbers: No numbers given in this paper for Metcalfe 1986. Metcalfe & Wiebe required subjects to be fully confident before answering; Hedne did not.
limits: Interpretation by the authors, not a test.
agent_relevance: Stopping rules that fire on felt closeness will accept wrong answers. A stop rule needs an external test.

source: Laukkonen & Tangen (2018) How to detect insight moments in problem solving experiments
finding: Two ways of detecting insight disagree: warmth suddenness and self-reported Aha. Per participant they agree; per problem they do not.
numbers: 80 undergraduates, 20 verbal insight problems, warmth every 10 s (1 to 10). Only 180 of 631 correctly solved problems had 2+ warmth ratings. Per-participant counts r=0.61 (n=51); per-problem r=0.08 (n=182, p=.235).
quote: a gradual warmth pattern does not necessarily mean that an insight did not occur
limits: Used a two-rating differential warmth; unsolved and wrong trials excluded; the authors' argument for self-report is conceptual, no ground truth.
agent_relevance: Warmth is a weak per-item signal; usable only in aggregate over many items. Suggests a trigger should use counts across many attempts, not one item.

source: Laukkonen & Tangen (2018) How to detect insight moments in problem solving experiments
finding: Gradual warmth was often followed by a self-reported Aha anyway. Perceived progress can be illusory, followed by a sudden strategy shift.
numbers: When warmth signalled sudden solution, 75.6% had a self-reported insight (24.4% did not). When warmth signalled gradual progress, 50.8% still reported insight (49.2% did not). Mean self-reported insights 5.28 (SD 2.74) vs warmth insights 4.85 (SD 2.7).
limits: Table is conditional on solved problems with 2+ ratings only (about 29% of solved items).
agent_relevance: A feeling of steady progress does not rule out the need to change approach. Progress and restructuring can both occur.

source: Kizilirmak et al. (2018) Feelings-of-warmth increase more abruptly for verbal riddles solved with aha
finding: Partial replication of Metcalfe & Wiebe on verbal riddles (German Compound Remote Associates). Warmth rose more steeply over the last two ratings when the riddle was solved with Aha than without.
numbers: N=36, 90 trials; warmth on a 0 to 4 scale about every 5 s, first at 6 to 7 s, limit 30 s. Solved items with 3+ ratings (27 participants): ROUND x AHA F(2,52)=15.63, p<.001, partial eta2=.375. Last-minus-third-to-last change 2.59 (SD .97) with Aha vs 1.43 (SD 1.07) without, t(26)=4.27, d=.82.
quote: a steeper increase for the last two FoW ratings when problems were solved with Aha!
limits: Warmth was split by Aha report, not by problem type. Interrupting the solving to ask warmth may alter the process. Subgroups of 20, 13 and 9 participants were descriptive. No a priori power analysis.
agent_relevance: Warmth after Aha rises steeply late; the late rise is a short fuse, not a long gradual one. A graded trigger would have little lead time in sudden cases.

source: Kizilirmak et al. (2018) Feelings-of-warmth increase more abruptly for verbal riddles solved with aha
finding: Aha reports were more common for self-generated than for presented solutions. Warmth on unsolved items stayed low and did not separate by Aha.
numbers: P(Aha) generated 0.76 (SD .27) vs presented 0.57 (SD .29), Wilcoxon T=179, p=.016. Unsolved items (34 participants): warmth rose slightly over rounds, F(5,165)=9.78, but no Aha difference, F(1,33)=1.66, p=.207; ratings stayed between 0 and 1.
limits: Authors note Hedne's Aha rate was 29% vs 76% here, which may explain the null in Hedne et al.
agent_relevance: On failing problems, felt warmth stays near zero. A low, flat signal on a stuck problem is informative about being stuck.

source: Durso, Rea & Dayton (1994) Graph-theoretic confirmation of restructuring during insight
finding: Restructuring was measured without self-report. Pathfinder networks built from relatedness judgments of 14 concepts differed completely between solvers and nonsolvers of a riddle puzzle (man asks for water, bartender points a shotgun).
numbers: Exp 1: solvers n=6, nonsolvers n=6, 91 pairs rated on a 10-point scale. Graph-distance matrix correlation solver vs nonsolver r=.00. Solvers' graph linked surprise-remedy and thank you-relieved, the keys to the solution.
limits: Very small groups; one puzzle (hiccoughs story); two-hour questioning limit.
agent_relevance: Solving changes the structure of the problem representation, not just a number. A restructuring is a different kind of change than a step of progress.

source: Durso, Rea & Dayton (1994) Graph-theoretic confirmation of restructuring during insight
finding: Control groups did not match the solvers' structure: listeners to the solvers' questions, a hiccough narrative, and solution-given groups looked like nonsolvers. Only generating the solution gave the solver structure.
numbers: Five more groups of 6 each. Correlation with solvers' graph: naive .09, story only .27*, listeners -.02, hiccough narrative -.04, solution given .13. With nonsolvers: .15, .39*, .68*, .23*, .38*. (* p<.05.)
quote: Apparently, one cannot easily share in the insight of a colleague, only in the results.
limits: Between-group, small cells; interpretation of the solution-given group is not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Handing a model a solution or hint is not the same as the model restructuring. Hints change output more than representation.

source: Durso, Rea & Dayton (1994) Graph-theoretic confirmation of restructuring during insight
finding: Exp 2: repeated relatedness judgments through the solving process showed the key concept pairs moved in two steps, not one jump. So some warning of restructuring exists before the solution.
numbers: N=10 subjects judged 12 pairs (2 insight, 2 related, 2 unrelated, 6 filler) at naive, story, every 10 min, and after solving. Phase x pair type F(6,4)=11.71, p<.05. Insight pairs moved first to an intermediate level t(9)=2.55, p<.05, then to high similarity t(9)=3.41, p<.01. 8 of 10 showed the story to solved-2 change (p=.055); all but 1 showed the drop between solved-1 and solved (p=.011).
quote: a long fuse warns of the impending reorganization
limits: N=10; repeated judging could itself cue the solver; one puzzle.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a gradual, hidden build-up before a sudden solution: a middle path between the two views. Gradual underlying change is possible even when felt warmth is flat.

source: Durso, Rea & Dayton (1994) Graph-theoretic confirmation of restructuring during insight
finding: Durso et al. cite Metcalfe (1986a) that self-reports about the chance of solving are unrelated to actual insight, so self-report after insight is unreliable too, which motivated an independent structural measure.
numbers: Cited: Bowers, Regehr & Balthazard (1990) found above-chance forced choice of solution-relevant stimuli before the solution could be named.
limits: Citation of other work, not new data here.
agent_relevance: Hidden partial knowledge exists that the solver cannot report. Do not use the model's own stated confidence as the only monitor.

source: Fedor, Szathmary & Ollinger (2015) Problem solving stages in the five square problem
finding: In the five-square matchstick problem, people's 'I'm stuck' button presses did not line up with behavioural impasse. Reports of impasse are an unreliable indicator.
numbers: N=129 (42 control, 87 impasse-monitoring group); after exclusions 101. Solve rate 55% control vs 49% button group, chi2(1)=0.14, p=.70. Presses: 33% of solvers (8/24) vs 79% of nonsolvers (34/43). Presses did not differ between plateaus/gaps and slopes, Z=0.63, p=.53.
limits: Online crowd sample (CrowdFlower), 15 min limit, 28 quick-solve participants excluded. Button may itself alter behaviour (no solve-rate difference found).
agent_relevance: Matches schema note that the model's own stuck signal is unreliable; use code counts (repeats, no change) for S6.

source: Fedor, Szathmary & Ollinger (2015) Problem solving stages in the five square problem
finding: Behaviour measures separate solvers from nonsolvers: repetition of positions was higher in nonsolvers, and most nonsolvers did not show the classic search-impasse-search pattern.
numbers: Repetition rate nonsolvers M=0.5 (SD .2) vs solvers 0.3 (SD .3), t(99)=5.13, d=1.03. Solvers (n=39): 49% classic search-impasse-search, 51% recurring search and impasse. Nonsolvers (n=62): 13% classic, 87% not. Insight reported by 74% of solvers vs 10% of nonsolvers, chi2=41.42.
limits: Stage labels (slopes, plateaus, gaps) were defined by the authors; the paper does not discuss progress monitoring theory directly.
agent_relevance: Repeated-state rate is a measurable and large (d about 1) failure predictor. Direct support for a repeated-state rule in S6.

source: Fedor, Szathmary & Ollinger (2015) Problem solving stages in the five square problem
finding: Search drifted toward the right area over time: moves near the cross fell and moves to possible solution positions rose between task halves.
numbers: Eight positions adjacent to the cross: M 51.4 to 38.4 (p=.009). Twelve possible solution positions: M 9.8 to 19.9 (p<.0001).
limits: Position counts are descriptive of the whole sample, not per solver.
agent_relevance: Even without felt progress, the search distribution shifts. A count of new states per window could show this.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem
finding: Aha experience is not tied to problem type: it appears in noninsight problems and varies by problem. Within classic insight problems, Aha correlates with accuracy; within noninsight problems, it barely does.
numbers: Exp 1 N=184, Exp 1a N=74, Exp 2 N=117. Accuracy-Aha r: insight .50/.40/.495; CRA .41/.40/.39; noninsight .02/.24/.19. Accuracy: insight 0.51/0.49/0.45; noninsight 0.54/0.64/0.56.
quote: problems can be solved with and without feelings of insight
limits: Warmth was not collected here. Table value for Exp 1a noninsight Aha mean (64.40) conflicts with the text, likely a typo.
agent_relevance: Problem-type labels (insight vs not) are weak guides to when to switch strategy; use behaviour.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem
finding: Cites Davidson (1995): 12 to 13% of noninsight problems showed an insight-like warmth pattern, and Metcalfe's claim that feeling suddenly close often marks a wrong solution.
numbers: Second-hand: Davidson 1995 gives 12 to 13% of noninsight problems with insight-pattern warmth. Davidson was not opened.
limits: Cited, not verified at the source.
agent_relevance: Pattern frequency is not 0 or 100 percent for either type, so a hard rule is brittle.

source: Wiley & Miller (2026) Aha! ratings as metacognitive judgments
finding: Aha ratings are judgments formed after the solution, using cues like fluency, not a readout of progress. They are higher for correct solutions and when the first move was correct.
numbers: N=377 students, 4 matchstick/coin problems, 1,164 analysed observations. Solve rates 33%, 48%, 34%, 17%. Aha-correctness F(1,1091)=112.17, partial R2=.09. Correct after a correct first move highest, F(2,1079)=71.48. Only 5 to 33% of correct solutions followed a wrong first move.
limits: No warmth or repeated progress ratings were collected; single 5-point item per problem; correlational.
agent_relevance: Late felt-certainty is partly a story built after the fact. Supports not trusting the model's after-the-fact confidence.

source: Chandolia, Kidd, Paladino & Smith (2026) Comparing Aha! moments in problem solving and generative ideation
finding: Aha strength was the same in problem solving and in generating ideas, and aha responses grew more likely later in a session and after longer pauses. Suddenness was assumed, not measured.
numbers: N=64, 64 verbal problems (CRA and PAT) at 15 s each; accuracy 39.67% (SD 13.86); aha rate 52.77% of correct trials; aha strength 3.04 in both tasks (Bayes factors support the null). Aha predicted by later intervals (beta .70) and longer pauses (beta .46).
limits: No warmth, impasse or progress measured; 5 participants excluded post hoc for all-5 ratings; fixed item order.
agent_relevance: Pauses precede sudden ideas. A long pause alone is not a stuck signal.

source: Working memory and representational change during insight problem solving (Frontiers in Psychology 2018, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2018.01864)
finding: Working-memory load probes were slower during non-insight than insight solving, consistent with non-insight solving needing a running control/monitoring process, while insight is a rare representational change.
numbers: Exp 1 (32+32): solution rate 77.9%; insight 64.06% vs non-insight 94.53%. Probe RT (s): baseline 0.79, insight 1.67, non-insight 1.93. Exp 2 (32+32): baseline 0.86, insight 1.35, non-insight 1.55.
limits: Does not name or test progress monitoring theory; trials under 30 s or over 5 min excluded; secondary-task method.
agent_relevance: Monitoring has a cost in working memory for incremental problems; for an agent, monitoring should be cheap code, not model text.

source: Ishikawa, Toshima & Mogi (2019) How and when? Metacognition and solution timing characterize an Aha experience of object recognition in hidden figures
finding: Intro describes warmth as the usual measure of felt distance to the solution. States that high warmth long before the solution, or a gradual rise, is likely a wrong answer (Metcalfe 1986).
numbers: Mooney image morph task with 100 steps; insight solutions more accurate and more confident. Aha strength correlated with suddenness and pleasure. Exact statistics were not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read; statistics not extracted.
agent_relevance: Same point: a rising felt-progress signal is a risk marker for wrong answers.

source: MacGregor, Ormerod & Chronicle (2001) Information processing and insight: a process model of performance on the nine-dot and related problems
finding: Progress monitoring theory (MacGregor, Ormerod & Chronicle): solvers use hill climbing or maximization to reduce the gap to the goal, and monitor progress against a criterion for satisfactory progress. When the criterion fails (not enough progress for the moves left), they drop the current approach and try alternatives, which is the source of insight on the nine-dot problem.
numbers: Not read this session (APA PsycNet returned only a loading page). No numbers recorded; do not quote from this line.
limits: Paywalled; a reader must check the original for N, move counts and solution rates.
agent_relevance: The direct theory for S6: a criterion on measured progress, tied to moves left, triggers a change. This is closer to a code-set rule than to felt warmth.

source: Ormerod, MacGregor & Chronicle (2002) Dynamics and constraints in insight problem solving; Novick & Sherman (2003) On the nature of insight solutions: skill differences in anagram solution; Smith & Kounios (1996) Sudden insight: all-or-none processing
finding: Follow-up studies named in the focus (Ormerod 2002, Novick & Sherman 2003) and the all-or-none anagram result (Smith & Kounios 1996) were identified by DOI but their full text could not be opened (paywalled). They are listed for the next pass.
numbers: No numbers recorded. Locations: Ormerod 10.1037/0278-7393.28.4.791; Novick & Sherman 10.1080/02724980244000288; Smith & Kounios 10.1037/0278-7393.22.6.1443.
limits: Unread; do not cite figures.
agent_relevance: Need the numbers for gradual versus sudden anagram solving before setting any graded-trigger threshold.
